spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Per **NIST SP 800-207**, zero-trust networking starts from a single premise: **network location does not imply trust**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Per-Request SPIFFE mTLS & Policy Authorization (Workload A (SVID) -> Policy Enforcer (PEP) -> OPA / AuthZ (PDP) -> Workload B); Zero Trust Identity Plane & Micro-Segmented Mesh (IdP / SPIRE CA -> Zero Trust Proxy -> Billing Pod -> Search Pod).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Sidecars enforce rich L7 HTTP/gRPC RBAC, JWT validation, and per-RPC telemetry uniformly across any language. **CA outage exceeding SVID TTL**: If SPIRE Server / Istiod is down longer than the 1-hour SVID lifetime, rotating certificates fail and all east-west mTLS traffic collapses simultaneously.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.

learningJourney.title: What is Zero Trust Networking

explanation.foundation:
The idea
Per **NIST SP 800-207**, zero-trust networking starts from a single premise: **network location does not imply trust**. Whether a packet originates from a coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a corporate office LAN, or `10.42.0.15` inside your own Kubernetes VPC, it is treated as untrusted until proven otherwise.
Instead of defending a static IP perimeter, zero trust binds security to **cryptographic identity** and **per-request context**:
1. **Workload Identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE)**: Every service instance proves who it is via node/platform attestation (AWS IID, K8s projected ServiceAccount token, or hardware TPM 2.0) and receives a short-lived X.509 certificate (SVID) encoding its canonical URI (`spiffe://trust-domain/ns/payments/sa/checkout`).
2. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)**: Both caller and callee present and verify SVIDs over TLS 1.3, guaranteeing confidentiality, integrity, and mutual authentication on every hop.
3. **Policy Decision & Enforcement (PDP/PEP)**: An in-line Policy Enforcement Point (Envoy proxy or Identity-Aware Proxy) evaluates each request against least-privilege rules combining *who* the caller is (SPIFFE ID), *who* the end-user is (verified OIDC JWT), and *what* action is requested (`POST /v1/refunds`).
explanation.core:
**Core Pillars:**
- Every workload receives a cryptographic identity—typically a SPIFFE ID (`spiffe://prod.internal/ns/payments/sa/ledger-api`) encoded in a short-lived X.509 SVID (1-hour to 24-hour TTL) rotated automatically without restarts.
- Transport encryption and mutual authentication (mTLS via TLS 1.3) ensure both client and server verify each other's certificates before exchanging a single application byte.
- Authorization is evaluated per request at L7 (Envoy RBAC, OPA/Rego, or Cilium eBPF) using `(caller_spiffe_id, user_jwt_claims, method, path)`—not source IP or CIDR blocks.
- User-to-service access uses Identity-Aware Proxies (OIDC/OAuth2 + device posture/TPM attestation) so compromised credentials on an unmanaged device are still rejected.
- Default-deny network posture: services reject all unauthenticated or unauthorized RPCs, and egress proxies restrict outbound calls to explicitly allowlisted domains/APIs.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Zero Trust Networking, watch how what is zero trust networking interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Zero Trust Networking (and what fails without it)

explanation.foundation: Traditional castle-and-moat networks assume anything inside `10.0.0.0/8` is benign. Once an attacker compromises a single CI runner, SSRF-vulnerable pod, or developer laptop over VPN, flat internal networks allow unconstrained lateral movement to databases and KMS endpoints. In ephemeral Kubernetes and multi-cloud clusters where pod IPs recycle every few minutes, IP allowlists are both operationally brittle and security-blind—only cryptographic identity scales.
explanation.core:
**Common Pitfalls:**
- Terminating TLS at the ingress/API gateway and running plaintext HTTP inside the cluster (`PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode left on indefinitely), leaving internal traffic exposed to sniffing and spoofing.
- Using IP-based `NetworkPolicy` alone without L7 workload identity—IPs are reused rapidly in Kubernetes and cannot distinguish two tenants or two endpoints on the same host.
- Granting wildcard authorization (`principals: ["*"]` or `methods: ["*"]`) to unblock a deploy and never scoping it down to least-privilege `(spiffe_id, method, path)`.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of Zero Trust Networking, watch how why we need zero trust networking (and what fails without it) interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Monitor `cert_expiry_seconds_remaining` with alerts at 50% TTL, configure overlapping rotation at 50% lifetime, run HA multi-AZ CA replicas, and keep intermediate TTLs (7–30 days) well above workload SVID TTLs (1–24h).

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge proxy, validate signed OIDC/JWT tokens at every L7 hop (or mint short-lived actor/delegation tokens), and bind L7 RBAC to both caller SPIFFE ID and JWT `aud`/`sub` claims.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Compile Rego policies into local Wasm or Envoy-native `RBAC` filters evaluated in-process (<0.5 ms), or co-locate OPA as a node/pod sidecar with fail-closed/cached bundle sync.

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Zero Trust Networking without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When untrusted callers cross a trust boundary, never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When Zero Trust Networking experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

learningJourney.title: Where Zero Trust Networking is used (and where to avoid it)

explanation.foundation: Think of **Where Zero Trust Networking is used (and where to avoid it)** as the intuition layer for Zero Trust Networking: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.
explanation.core: Zero Trust Networking delivers the highest leverage at well-defined architectural boundaries. Use it for multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, where zero trust networking is used (and where to avoid it) becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

comparison.benefits: Multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.
comparison.costs: Ultra-low-latency (<100 microsecond) IPC or kernel-bypass HPC/HFT fabrics (RDMA/DPDK) inside a physically isolated single-tenant rack where per-packet TLS/sidecar proxy hops blow the latency budget.

comparison.benefits: Hybrid or multi-cloud architectures (e.g., AWS EKS calling on-prem Postgres or GCP Cloud Run) where traffic traverses untrusted WANs without relying on brittle site-to-site IPsec tunnels.
comparison.costs: Legacy embedded OT/SCADA hardware incapable of TLS 1.3 or short-lived certificate rotation, which must instead be isolated behind terminating zero-trust gateways.

comparison.benefits: Remote engineering access to internal admin panels, CI/CD, and production APIs via Identity-Aware Proxies (Cloudflare Access, Google BeyondCorp IAP, Tailscale) instead of broad corporate VPNs.
comparison.costs: Single-process monoliths or isolated dev sandboxes where adding a full SPIRE + Envoy control plane introduces operational complexity without meaningful trust boundaries.

comparison.choice: Stopping Lateral Movement in Kubernetes with SPIRE + Envoy mTLS
comparison.costs: Requires strict operational guardrails and observability.

comparison.choice: Replacing Corporate VPN with BeyondCorp Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
comparison.costs: Requires strict operational guardrails and observability.

learningJourney.title: How Zero Trust Networking works under the hood & reference implementation

explanation.foundation:
Concrete walkthrough
Trace an engineer triggering a refund via an internal support tool (`https://support.corp.internal`) backed by `support-bff` -> `payments-api` in Kubernetes:
1. **User & Device Attestation**: The engineer's browser hits the **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)**. IAP redirects to the OIDC IdP, verifies a hardware FIDO2 passkey plus MDM device-posture claim (`disk_encrypted=true, os_patched=true`), and attaches a 15-minute signed JWT (`sub=alice@corp.com, role=support_l2`) before forwarding to `support-bff`.
2. **Workload Identity Issuance**: On the Kubernetes worker node, the local **SPIRE Agent** attests `support-bff`'s pod UID and projected ServiceAccount token against the Kubelet, then delivers a 1-hour X.509 SVID (`spiffe://prod.corp/ns/support/sa/support-bff`) over a Unix domain socket via Envoy SDS.
3. **mTLS Handshake**: `support-bff` calls `https://payments-api.prod.svc:8443/v1/refunds`. Its local Envoy sidecar initiates TLS 1.3 mTLS with `payments-api`'s Envoy sidecar. Both sides validate the SPIFFE trust-bundle root CA and SAN URI (`~1.4 ms` new handshake, `<0.1 ms` on pooled HTTP/2 connection).
4. **L7 Policy Evaluation**: `payments-api`'s Envoy PEP inspects the verified peer SPIFFE ID (`support-bff`), the forwarded OIDC JWT (`role=support_l2`), and the HTTP route (`POST /v1/refunds`). Its compiled RBAC/OPA rule (`allow if peer == support-bff AND jwt.role in ['support_l2', 'finance']`) passes in `0.3 ms` and forwards the request to the `payments-api` container over `localhost`.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
## Reference implementation (Python — Constant-Time Signature & Expiry Verification)
```python
# Constant-time HMAC / token expiry verification (Python)
import hmac, hashlib, time
def verify_signed_token(payload: bytes, signature_hex: str, secret: bytes, exp_ts: int) -> bool:
    if time.time() > exp_ts:
        return False
    expected = hmac.new(secret, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature_hex)
```

### Operational Guidelines
- Core mental model: Never trust a packet because it arrived on a private RFC 1918 subnet; authenticate every caller's short-lived X.509 SVID over mTLS and authorize the exact HTTP/gRPC action on every service boundary.
- Avoid trap: Terminating TLS at the ingress/API gateway and running plaintext HTTP inside the cluster (`PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode left on indefinitely), leaving internal traffic exposed to sniffing and spoofing.
- Avoid trap: Using IP-based `NetworkPolicy` alone without L7 workload identity—IPs are reused rapidly in Kubernetes and cannot distinguish two tenants or two endpoints on the same host.
- When to reach for it: Multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.

explanation.foundation: Think of **Alternatives & trade-offs for Zero Trust Networking** as the intuition layer for Zero Trust Networking: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.
explanation.core: Evaluating Zero Trust Networking against alternatives requires balancing latency, operational overhead, failure blast radius, and cost. Sidecars enforce rich L7 HTTP/gRPC RBAC, JWT validation, and per-RPC telemetry uniformly across any language.
explanation.deepDive: Under heavy load or partial failure, alternatives & trade-offs for zero trust networking becomes a critical lever for predictable latency and correctness. Zero-trust networking replaces implicit IP- and VLAN-based perimeter trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE/mTLS), continuous device/user attestation, and per-request L7 authorization (Envoy/OPA) on every hop.

comparison.choice: Sidecar Proxy (Envoy/Istio) vs. Ambient / Kernel eBPF (Cilium)
comparison.benefits: Sidecars enforce rich L7 HTTP/gRPC RBAC, JWT validation, and per-RPC telemetry uniformly across any language.
comparison.costs: Adds ~1–2 ms p99 latency per hop and ~50–100 MB RAM + 0.05–0.15 vCPU per pod; ambient/eBPF modes cut memory by moving L4 mTLS to node-level ztunnel/kernel.

comparison.choice: Short-Lived SVIDs (1h TTL) vs. Long-Lived Certs + CRL/OCSP
comparison.benefits: Eliminates brittle CRL/OCSP revocation lookups on the hot path—stolen certs expire automatically within 60 minutes.
comparison.costs: Requires a highly available, low-latency local SDS/SPIRE Agent on every node; if the CA control plane stalls for >1h, workloads lose valid certs simultaneously.

comparison.choice: Strict Default-Deny Policy vs. Developer Velocity
comparison.benefits: Prevents shadow APIs and accidental over-privileged service-to-service paths from reaching production.
comparison.costs: New microservice integrations fail with `403` until explicit `AuthorizationPolicy` manifests are reviewed and deployed in CI/CD.

learningJourney.title: Production architecture & hardening for Zero Trust Networking

explanation.foundation:
Failure modes
- **CA outage exceeding SVID TTL**: If SPIRE Server / Istiod is down longer than the 1-hour SVID lifetime, rotating certificates fail and all east-west mTLS traffic collapses simultaneously.
- **Permissive mode drift**: Teams enable `mTLS: PERMISSIVE` during migration and forget to flip to `STRICT`, allowing unauthenticated plaintext lateral movement.
- **Header spoofing (Confused Deputy)**: Backends trust `X-Forwarded-User` headers from any mTLS peer without validating who is allowed to assert end-user identity.
- **Centralized PDP latency/outage**: Making synchronous remote calls to an external OPA server on every RPC turns policy evaluation into a single point of failure.
explanation.core:
Practical checklist
- [ ] Enforce `STRICT` TLS 1.3 mTLS across all production namespaces; verify zero plaintext listeners remain.
- [ ] Issue short-lived workload SVIDs (1–24h TTL) via SPIRE or mesh CA with automatic rotation at 50% lifetime and 500 ms max NTP/Chrony clock skew.
- [ ] Scope Envoy `Sidecar` / `AuthorizationPolicy` manifests to explicit `(caller_spiffe_id, method, path)` tuples—never `principals: ["*"]`.
- [ ] Validate OIDC/JWT signatures and strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge and service boundaries.
- [ ] Run OPA/RBAC evaluation in-process (Envoy native RBAC or Wasm) rather than synchronous remote PDP calls.
- [ ] Lock down pod egress with default-deny egress proxies and maintain a documented break-glass runbook for IdP/CA outages.

learningJourney.title: What is Zero Trust Networking
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Zero Trust Networking works from first principles.
learningJourney.explanation:
## The idea
Per **NIST SP 800-207**, zero-trust networking starts from a single premise: **network location does not imply trust**. Whether a packet originates from a coffee-shop Wi-Fi, a corporate office LAN, or `10.42.0.15` inside your own Kubernetes VPC, it is treated as untrusted until proven otherwise.
Instead of defending a static IP perimeter, zero trust binds security to **cryptographic identity** and **per-request context**:
1. **Workload Identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE)**: Every service instance proves who it is via node/platform attestation (AWS IID, K8s projected ServiceAccount token, or hardware TPM 2.0) and receives a short-lived X.509 certificate (SVID) encoding its canonical URI (`spiffe://trust-domain/ns/payments/sa/checkout`).
2. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)**: Both caller and callee present and verify SVIDs over TLS 1.3, guaranteeing confidentiality, integrity, and mutual authentication on every hop.
3. **Policy Decision & Enforcement (PDP/PEP)**: An in-line Policy Enforcement Point (Envoy proxy or Identity-Aware Proxy) evaluates each request against least-privilege rules combining *who* the caller is (SPIFFE ID), *who* the end-user is (verified OIDC JWT), and *what* action is requested (`POST /v1/refunds`).

**Core Pillars:**
- Every workload receives a cryptographic identity—typically a SPIFFE ID (`spiffe://prod.internal/ns/payments/sa/ledger-api`) encoded in a short-lived X.509 SVID (1-hour to 24-hour TTL) rotated automatically without restarts.
- Transport encryption and mutual authentication (mTLS via TLS 1.3) ensure both client and server verify each other's certificates before exchanging a single application byte.
- Authorization is evaluated per request at L7 (Envoy RBAC, OPA/Rego, or Cilium eBPF) using `(caller_spiffe_id, user_jwt_claims, method, path)`—not source IP or CIDR blocks.
- User-to-service access uses Identity-Aware Proxies (OIDC/OAuth2 + device posture/TPM attestation) so compromised credentials on an unmanaged device are still rejected.
- Default-deny network posture: services reject all unauthenticated or unauthorized RPCs, and egress proxies restrict outbound calls to explicitly allowlisted domains/APIs.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Zero Trust Networking (and what fails without it)
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Zero Trust Networking under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
Traditional castle-and-moat networks assume anything inside `10.0.0.0/8` is benign. Once an attacker compromises a single CI runner, SSRF-vulnerable pod, or developer laptop over VPN, flat internal networks allow unconstrained lateral movement to databases and KMS endpoints. In ephemeral Kubernetes and multi-cloud clusters where pod IPs recycle every few minutes, IP allowlists are both operationally brittle and security-blind—only cryptographic identity scales.

**Common Pitfalls:**
- Terminating TLS at the ingress/API gateway and running plaintext HTTP inside the cluster (`PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode left on indefinitely), leaving internal traffic exposed to sniffing and spoofing.
- Using IP-based `NetworkPolicy` alone without L7 workload identity—IPs are reused rapidly in Kubernetes and cannot distinguish two tenants or two endpoints on the same host.
- Granting wildcard authorization (`principals: ["*"]` or `methods: ["*"]`) to unblock a deploy and never scoping it down to least-privilege `(spiffe_id, method, path)`.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Monitor `cert_expiry_seconds_remaining` with alerts at 50% TTL, configure overlapping rotation at 50% lifetime, run HA multi-AZ CA replicas, and keep intermediate TTLs (7–30 days) well above workload SVID TTLs (1–24h).

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge proxy, validate signed OIDC/JWT tokens at every L7 hop (or mint short-lived actor/delegation tokens), and bind L7 RBAC to both caller SPIFFE ID and JWT `aud`/`sub` claims.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Compile Rego policies into local Wasm or Envoy-native `RBAC` filters evaluated in-process (<0.5 ms), or co-locate OPA as a node/pod sidecar with fail-closed/cached bundle sync.

learningJourney.title: Where Zero Trust Networking is used (and where to avoid it)
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.
learningJourney.explanation: Zero Trust Networking delivers the highest leverage at well-defined architectural boundaries. Use it for multi-tenant or regulated microservices (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2) in Kubernetes/ECS where lateral movement after a single pod compromise must be blocked by default-deny L7 policies.

learningJourney.title: How Zero Trust Networking works under the hood & reference implementation
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.
learningJourney.explanation:
## Concrete walkthrough
Trace an engineer triggering a refund via an internal support tool (`https://support.corp.internal`) backed by `support-bff` -> `payments-api` in Kubernetes:
1. **User & Device Attestation**: The engineer's browser hits the **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)**. IAP redirects to the OIDC IdP, verifies a hardware FIDO2 passkey plus MDM device-posture claim (`disk_encrypted=true, os_patched=true`), and attaches a 15-minute signed JWT (`sub=alice@corp.com, role=support_l2`) before forwarding to `support-bff`.
2. **Workload Identity Issuance**: On the Kubernetes worker node, the local **SPIRE Agent** attests `support-bff`'s pod UID and projected ServiceAccount token against the Kubelet, then delivers a 1-hour X.509 SVID (`spiffe://prod.corp/ns/support/sa/support-bff`) over a Unix domain socket via Envoy SDS.
3. **mTLS Handshake**: `support-bff` calls `https://payments-api.prod.svc:8443/v1/refunds`. Its local Envoy sidecar initiates TLS 1.3 mTLS with `payments-api`'s Envoy sidecar. Both sides validate the SPIFFE trust-bundle root CA and SAN URI (`~1.4 ms` new handshake, `<0.1 ms` on pooled HTTP/2 connection).
4. **L7 Policy Evaluation**: `payments-api`'s Envoy PEP inspects the verified peer SPIFFE ID (`support-bff`), the forwarded OIDC JWT (`role=support_l2`), and the HTTP route (`POST /v1/refunds`). Its compiled RBAC/OPA rule (`allow if peer == support-bff AND jwt.role in ['support_l2', 'finance']`) passes in `0.3 ms` and forwards the request to the `payments-api` container over `localhost`.

learningJourney.title: Production architecture & hardening for Zero Trust Networking
learningJourney.purpose: Production architecture: see how the components compose end to end under real load.
learningJourney.explanation:
## Failure modes
- **CA outage exceeding SVID TTL**: If SPIRE Server / Istiod is down longer than the 1-hour SVID lifetime, rotating certificates fail and all east-west mTLS traffic collapses simultaneously.
- **Permissive mode drift**: Teams enable `mTLS: PERMISSIVE` during migration and forget to flip to `STRICT`, allowing unauthenticated plaintext lateral movement.
- **Header spoofing (Confused Deputy)**: Backends trust `X-Forwarded-User` headers from any mTLS peer without validating who is allowed to assert end-user identity.
- **Centralized PDP latency/outage**: Making synchronous remote calls to an external OPA server on every RPC turns policy evaluation into a single point of failure.

## Practical checklist
- [ ] Enforce `STRICT` TLS 1.3 mTLS across all production namespaces; verify zero plaintext listeners remain.
- [ ] Issue short-lived workload SVIDs (1–24h TTL) via SPIRE or mesh CA with automatic rotation at 50% lifetime and 500 ms max NTP/Chrony clock skew.
- [ ] Scope Envoy `Sidecar` / `AuthorizationPolicy` manifests to explicit `(caller_spiffe_id, method, path)` tuples—never `principals: ["*"]`.
- [ ] Validate OIDC/JWT signatures and strip untrusted `X-User-*` headers at the edge and service boundaries.
- [ ] Run OPA/RBAC evaluation in-process (Envoy native RBAC or Wasm) rather than synchronous remote PDP calls.
- [ ] Lock down pod egress with default-deny egress proxies and maintain a documented break-glass runbook for IdP/CA outages.
